title: Warfarin-induced skin necrosis: underlying protein C deficiency
vignette: A 50-year-old woman comes to the emergency department due to a large, painful skin lesion. She does not remember sustaining any trauma. She was recently diagnosed with atrial fibrillation and started on treatment with warfarin. The patient noticed the lesion about a day and a half after starting the medication. Temperature is 36.7 C (98 F), blood pressure is 130/82 mm Hg, and pulse is 88/min and irregularly irregular. Physical examination shows a sharply demarcated, purpuric, necrotic skin lesion over the extremity. The remainder of the skin examination is normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's skin lesion?

clues.note: Warfarin can cause skin necrosis early in therapy, especially in patients with an underlying hypercoagulable tendency.

clues.text: noticed the lesion about a day and a half after starting the medication
clues.note: Skin necrosis appearing within the first few days of warfarin is the classic timing of warfarin-induced skin necrosis (from a transient hypercoagulable state).

clues.text: sharply demarcated, purpuric, necrotic skin lesion
clues.note: A sharply demarcated purpuric/necrotic lesion from microvascular thrombosis is characteristic of warfarin-induced skin necrosis.

whatMatters: Sharply demarcated necrotic skin lesions appearing 1-5 days after starting warfarin = WARFARIN-INDUCED SKIN NECROSIS. It results from an early, excessive fall in PROTEIN C (a vitamin K-dependent anticoagulant with a SHORT half-life), creating a transient HYPERCOAGULABLE state; patients with underlying PROTEIN C DEFICIENCY are at greatest risk. Answer D.
strategy: Recall warfarin pharmacology: it inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X AND the anticoagulants protein C and S. Protein C (like factor VII) has a SHORT half-life, so it drops FIRST, briefly tipping toward thrombosis; in protein C deficiency this is exaggerated -> microvascular thrombosis and skin necrosis. Reject antithrombin deficiency (VTE/heparin resistance, not warfarin necrosis), autoimmune (vasculitis - not this), allergic drug reaction (diffuse eruption/SJS), and vitamin K deficiency (bleeding, not thrombosis).

eliminations.label: Allergic drug reaction - diffuse eruption, not focal necrosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: immune-mediated hypersensitivity (morbilliform rash, urticaria, or Stevens-Johnson syndrome). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: warfarin skin necrosis is a THROMBOTIC, sharply demarcated necrotic lesion, not a diffuse allergic eruption. ✅ Correct if: a drug-induced hypersensitivity rash/SJS.

eliminations.label: Antithrombin deficiency - VTE + heparin resistance
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a hypercoagulable state causing venous thromboembolism and resistance to heparin. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: warfarin does not affect antithrombin, and antithrombin deficiency doesn't cause warfarin skin necrosis (that's protein C/S). ✅ Correct if: recurrent VTE with poor response to heparin.

eliminations.label: Autoimmune phenomena - vasculitis (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: immune-mediated small-vessel vasculitis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the temporal link to warfarin initiation and the microthrombotic mechanism point to protein C-related necrosis, not an autoimmune vasculitis. ✅ Correct if: palpable purpura with vasculitic histology unrelated to warfarin.

eliminations.label: Vitamin K deficiency - causes bleeding, not thrombosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: deficiency of vitamin K (impairs factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C/S). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it increases warfarin's effect and causes BLEEDING; it doesn't create the hypercoagulable microthrombosis of skin necrosis. ✅ Correct if: bleeding with prolonged PT (malabsorption/antibiotics).

reasoning: Sharply demarcated necrotic skin lesion 1-2 days after starting warfarin = warfarin-induced skin necrosis
Warfarin inhibits vitamin K-dependent factors AND protein C/S; protein C has a short half-life and falls first
This transient hypercoagulable state (exaggerated in protein C deficiency) thromboses dermal microvessels
mechanism: Warfarin inhibits epoxide reductase (which regenerates vitamin K), reducing gamma-carboxylation of the vitamin K-dependent PROCOAGULANT factors II, VII, IX, and X AND the natural ANTICOAGULANTS protein C and protein S. Because factor VII and PROTEIN C have SHORT half-lives, their activity falls FIRST - before the longer-lived procoagulant factors (II, IX, X) are depleted - creating a TRANSIENT HYPERCOAGULABLE state in the first days of therapy. In patients with underlying PROTEIN C DEFICIENCY (or protein S deficiency), this early loss of anticoagulant activity is exaggerated, causing THROMBOSIS of dermal microvessels and hemorrhagic SKIN NECROSIS - classically over fatty areas (breast, thigh, buttocks) 1-5 days after starting warfarin. Prevention is to overlap (bridge) with HEPARIN during warfarin initiation. The distractors don't fit: allergic reactions cause diffuse eruptions; antithrombin deficiency causes VTE/heparin resistance (unrelated to warfarin); autoimmune vasculitis is a different mechanism; and vitamin K deficiency causes bleeding, not thrombosis.

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm/Heme > warfarin-induced skin necrosis: early protein C depletion (short half-life) -> transient hypercoagulable state; underlying protein C (or S) deficiency; bridge with heparin; treat by stopping warfarin + FFP/protein C.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Skin necrosis days after starting warfarin = protein C deficiency (transient hypercoagulability).

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on protein C/S, vitamin K-dependent factors, epoxide reductase, half-life, or hypercoagulable state? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Antithrombin deficiency = VTE/heparin resistance; allergic = diffuse eruption; vitamin K deficiency = bleeding; autoimmune = vasculitis.

difficulty.label: 🖼️ Imaging / diagram
difficulty.text: On the photo: a sharply demarcated, purpuric/necrotic lesion over the extremity (microvascular thrombosis). Anchor: 'necrotic skin days after warfarin start = protein C deficiency.'

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: warfarin skin necrosis = protein C deficiency (short half-life drops first); prevent by heparin bridging.

memoryHook: Warfarin knocks out protein C first (short half-life), so blood turns briefly sticky - in a protein C-deficient patient, skin clots and dies days after the first dose; heparin bridging prevents it.
